questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How to make fresh noodles at home
Why pasta is healthier than noodles
How noodles spread and changed in different countries
The life of the explorer Marco Polo
questions.why: They look at how noodles spread from China and how the US and Japan created new varieties.

options: Udon, which are big and thick
Ramen with beef
Dried noodles from a packet with hot water
Spicy rice noodles
questions.why: Beth says her favourite are udon – 'the big thick ones'.

questions.q: How did noodle recipes spread, according to Beth?
options: Chinese chefs opened restaurants in Europe and taught people to cook
They were written in famous cookbooks
Italian explorers brought them home
Traders on the Silk Road took them to new places
questions.why: She says noodle recipes were spread by traders on the ancient Silk Road.

questions.q: According to author Jen Lin-Liu, why was the Marco Polo story created?
options: To teach children about Chinese history
To help a pasta association sell more dried pasta
To explain how pasta was really invented
To make Chinese noodles more popular than pasta in Italy
questions.why: She says a new pasta association wanted to promote dried pasta, so they came up with the story.

questions.q: What happened after the Marco Polo story spread in the US?
options: People stopped eating noodles
Pasta sales went up
Italy banned dried pasta
Chinese restaurants closed
questions.why: Neil says 'it worked – sales of pasta jumped as a result'.

questions.q: How much ramen does blogger Frank Striegl eat?
options: About three bowls every single week
One bowl every week
More than 300 bowls a year
Three bowls a day
questions.why: Beth says he eats over 300 bowls of ramen a year.

questions.q: According to Frank, how did ramen develop in Japan?
options: Chefs changed Chinese noodle dishes to make them more Japanese
It was invented by Japanese farmers
It came from Italian pasta dishes
It was copied exactly from Chinese recipes without making any changes
questions.why: He says chefs loved Chinese noodle dishes but decided to 'tweak them' to be more Japanese.

questions.q: What does Frank find fascinating about ramen?
options: It has not changed at all for hundreds of years, like sushi
It is the cheapest food in Japan
It is more traditional than sushi
It keeps changing, and chefs can try new ideas
questions.why: He says ramen 'continues to evolve' and 'it's OK to push the boundaries'.
